Subject: Dedicated throughput + committed pricing for BrightCore

Hi Olga,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the latency looked great. We ran the internal model projections and want to explore a dedicated reserved commit for production. High level: ~18M generation calls/month, average 450 tokens/request (prompt+response), 99th-percentile concurrency spikes up to ~180 concurrent requests, typical context length ~3k tokens for long-tail queries.

Our questions:
- What committed GPU pool size would you recommend to meet a 95th percentile per-request P99 latency of <300ms for the above profile?
- What pricing/discounts do you offer for a 12-month reserved commit?
- Are there packaging options (burst credits, hybrid pool) if we want some headroom for spikes?

I attached our workload CSV (brightcore_workload_estimate.xlsx). Procurement will be on the thread (Tara) for contract steps once we have a target number.

—Alex
VP Product, BrightCore Analytics
From: olga_petrov@redwood.com

Date: 2026-02-15T09:04:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated throughput + committed pricing for BrightCore

Hi Alex — thanks for the detail and for sharing the sheet. I ran a first-pass sizing with the infra team and put together a conservative recommendation. Key assumptions: 70B-class FP16 model (production mix), average 450 tokens per call, token generation speed of ~350 tokens/s per A100-80GB equivalent when servicing smaller batches, and an objective to keep tail latency within your P99 goal by keeping queuing minimal.

Short answer (conservative): 8x A100-80GB equivalent GPUs with an autoscale buffer (burst credits) to double for short periods. That maps to a steady reserved footprint that handles ~140 concurrent requests at your token profile with latency headroom; burst to 16 GPUs for sustained short spikes up to ~300 concurrency.

We can reduce the steady commit to 6x GPUs if you accept slightly higher queueing at absolute peak (P99 pushes toward 320–350ms) and apply local KV caching for repeated prompts (expected 8–12% token reduction).

I'll loop Marissa for pricing and packaging options.

Best,
Olga
Principal Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference

Hi Alex / Tara — thanks, happy to take pricing. Based on Olga's sizing (8x steady, burst to 16x) we can offer the following commercial structure for a 12-month reserved commit: 

Option A — Predictable Commit (preferred)
- 8 GPU steady reserved pool (A100-80GB equivalent)
- Monthly commit: $110,000/month (annualized $1,320,000)
- Includes 24 hours/month of burst credits to scale to 16 GPUs for short periods; additional burst billed at usage-based rate
- 18% enterprise discount applied to list for first-year commit
- 99.9% availability SLA for the dedicated pool

Option B — Right-sized + Headroom
- 6 GPU steady reserved pool
- Monthly commit: $87,500/month
- Burst credits: 72 hours/month to scale to 16 GPUs
- 14% discount applied to list
- Autoscale policy and telemetry dashboard included to tune before quarterly reviews

Notes / negotiating levers:
- We can move to a stepped pricing model (lower effective price at 9+ months committed) or add an upfront payment to deepen discounts to ~22–24% if that helps procurement.
- If you accept model quantization (int8) for non-critical routes, we can reduce GPU footprint by ~20% and pass along equivalent savings.

Attaching a redlineable term sheet (BrightCore_Redwood_MA.pdf) and the workload estimate you provided. Let me know which option you want to take to procurement/corporate finance.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole

Quick technical clarification and tuning note from infra:
- The assumed token-generation throughput per-GPU varies substantially with model sequence length and batching. Your 3k context length for a subset means we should split traffic by model route: long-context calls (3k tokens) go to a larger memory-optimized instance (H100-like) — those consume more GPU memory/bandwidth and reduce per-GPU concurrent capacity.
- Recommendation: logical routing with two variants: 
  1) Standard route (95% of traffic): 70B-class quantized FP16 on A100-class nodes — served from the steady 6–8 GPU majority.
  2) Long-context route (5% of traffic): H100-like nodes with higher memory to avoid KV spill; reserve 1–2 GPUs in the pool of the burstable capacity specifically for these calls.

Operational impact: slightly higher effective reserved headcount if long-context share grows — budget for an extra 1 GPU to keep P99 guarantees during growth (i.e., 9 steady -> burst to 18 in peak scenario).

I'll work with Olga to produce a traffic-split runbook (routes, prompts to cache, and eval prompts to watch for quality regressions) if you decide to proceed.

—Karthik
Senior Infrastructure Architect — Redwood Inference
